topics.topic: Required confirmation-binding guarantee: exact input equality or equality under a stated cryptographic collision-resistance assumption, and its test/review scope
questions: What guarantee must make digest equality stand for equality of the inputs shown: literal collision-free equality, or computational security from a collision-resistant cryptographic digest over an unambiguous encoding? The text must also say whether A13 Required test 12's statement that every changed submission is refused is absolute or subject to that cryptographic assumption.

Does a matching digest guarantee that the confirming transaction uses exactly the file, picks, names, aliases and Customer values shown, or may different values with the same digest count as bound? A16 requires the former, while changed A13 defines binding only by digest equality without deciding the encoding or collision guarantee needed to support it.

What precise guarantee does “binds what its step showed” assert after removal of A13's unambiguous-encoding and collision-resistance requirement: exact equality for all allowed inputs, or equality subject to a stated cryptographic collision assumption? The security review cannot close this category until the A13 guarantee is stated.

Does the reopened security review still require a general guarantee that a confirmation binds exactly what its step showed, or does it accept only the finite examples exercised by test 12 despite A13 defining input binding solely by digest equality?

bases.rests_on:
One project has one canonical `project_id` in production, used by Cabinet,
PresuPro and Client Portal. Test instances use an identity space of their own
and hold no production personal data. A project crosses into production only by
an explicit import whose mapping the owner checks — the projects already held
by the running instances included (migration) — and it keeps its links:
customer, object, rooms, pointers.

witness.initial: An owner session holds a pending import confirmation for a clean mapping made from inputs X, and distinct permitted inputs Y have the same stored digest under a digest construction the texts do not exclude.
events: Registry shows the import confirmation step for X and keeps only the digest of its inputs.
The owner submits the pending confirmation value with Y.
The confirming transaction builds a clean mapping from Y.
outcomes: A13 treats Y as bound because its digest equals the pending digest, so the transaction may import Y.
A16 requires the applied mapping to be the one the step showed, so only X may be imported and Y must not proceed.
witness.observer: The owner and readers of the imported Projects, Customers, Rooms and pointers.
basis:
The owner uploads the export file (R0-72) in the owner interface. Registry
   reads it as data (A19) and answers, without changing anything, each
   project the file holds with its id and status.

The owner confirms that mapping in the confirmation
   step (A13 rule 6); the confirmation applies the file of that digest, the
   picks, names, aliases and Customer values the mapping showed, nothing
   else; a file no longer kept is refused and must be uploaded again.

A submission
   carries it when it passes the owner session and CSRF checks (A04 rule 6,
   stage 1) and gives a value equal to the pending one; from there on,
   whatever the answer — a binding to another action or input included — the
   pending value is used up.

judgement.why: State 2 owns the observable equality guarantee, but generation owns the canonical typed encoding, domain separation, digest interface and algorithm that realize it; the later public API already keeps action, target and shown version separately and digests the inputs.
options: Store action, target and revision separately and digest only a canonical encoding of the inputs.
Digest one canonical, domain-separated encoding of action, target, revision and inputs.
Use separate domain-separated digests for the identity fields and the inputs.
Use a canonical type-tagged, length-delimited encoding and a named cryptographic digest.
Use a strictly specified canonical serialization such as canonical JSON or CBOR and a named cryptographic digest.
Use a dedicated generated digest recipe or provider symbol whose contract defines canonicalization and digest production.
consequences: Separate comparisons are simpler to inspect but must remain consistent with the one observable refusal rule and the prohibition on retaining input values.
A complete-tuple digest makes binding atomic but requires canonical typed representations for every field.
Separate digests isolate representations but add state and comparison paths.
A bespoke type-tagged encoding is compact and auditable but needs precise rules for every type and boundary.
A standard canonical serialization reduces bespoke encoding but introduces serialization and dependency constraints.
A dedicated generated recipe centralizes production and checking but requires every confirmation producer and checker to use the same symbol.
